What’s happening is a common SEO/spam hack:
- normal visitors may see the real site
- users arriving from Google or other referrers get redirected to spam/offline pages
- Google may also show spammy titles or prefixes because the attacker injected code into your pages or templates

What to do:
1. Change all passwords immediately
   - hosting/control panel
   - FTP/SFTP
   - CMS admin accounts
   - database user
   - email accounts tied to the site

2. Check for injected code
   - search your files for `base64_decode`, `eval`, `gzinflate`, `str_rot13`, `preg_replace` with `/e`
   - inspect `.htaccess`, `index.php`, template files, and any recently modified files
   - if using Joomla, compare core files against fresh copies

3. Reinstall clean core files
   - replace Joomla core files with a fresh download
   - keep only your verified templates/extensions, and inspect them carefully

4. Check the database too
   - attackers often insert redirects or spam titles into template settings or content records

5. Review server logs
   - look for unexpected file changes, suspicious POST requests, and unknown admin logins

6. If possible, restore from a known-good backup
   - ideally from before the infection

7. Tell your hosting provider
   - on shared hosting, another compromised account can also be involved

Yes, but not with `Disallow: /` alone.

If you add:

Disallow: /

to `robots.txt`, Googlebot is told not to crawl any pages on your site, including the homepage. So that will prevent indexing of the whole site, not just the other pages.

If you want:
- homepage indexed
- all other pages not indexed

then use one of these approaches:

1. On the homepage, allow normal indexing:
   <meta name="robots" content="INDEX, FOLLOW" />

2. On every other page, add:
   <meta name="robots" content="NOINDEX, NOFOLLOW" />

Important note:
- `robots.txt` controls crawling, not indexing directly.
- `noindex` works only if Google can crawl the page.
- If you block a page in `robots.txt`, Google may not see the `noindex` tag.

So the best setup is:
- leave the homepage crawlable
- put `noindex` on all other pages
- do not use `Disallow: /` if you want the homepage indexed

Here’s a corrected version of those assumptions, with the important caveats:

1. If a page is crawled by Google, it automatically gets into the index.  
False. A page can be crawled but still not indexed. Common reasons include:
- `noindex` meta tag or HTTP header
- thin/duplicate/low-value content
- canonicalization to another URL
- quality/spam signals
- blocked resources or rendering issues

Also, a page blocked by `robots.txt` usually cannot be crawled, but it can still sometimes end up indexed if Google discovers the URL from links and has enough signals.

2. An indexed page always gets a ranking.  
Mostly true in the sense that if a page is in the index, Google can show it for some queries. But not always:
- it may rank extremely poorly
- it may only rank for very specific queries
- it may be removed or suppressed due to spam/manual actions
- it may be in the index but not practically visible in results

3. A page that is not referenced by any other pages and does not appear in a sitemap will never be crawled or indexed.  
False. It is less likely to be discovered, but not impossible. Google can still find it via:
- external links
- direct submission in Search Console
- previously known URLs
- other discovery signals

If a URL has no links and no sitemap entry, Google usually won’t find it easily, but “never” is too strong.

4. Google will update its index and ranking for some sites faster than for others.  
True. Crawl frequency and refresh speed vary by site based on:
- site authority/trust
- how often content changes
- internal linking
- site structure
- server performance
- crawl demand and crawl budget

5. More popular sites are indexed and ranked faster than less popular sites.  
Generally true, but “popular” is not the exact factor. More important signals are:
- stronger backlink profiles
- higher trust/authority
- frequent updates
- good internal linking
- overall site quality

So yes, well-known and well-linked sites are usually crawled and refreshed faster than small or new sites.

If you’re moving content from a subdomain to a subdirectory and want to preserve SEO as much as possible, the key is a proper 301 redirect from every old URL to the matching new URL.

Recommended approach:

1. Set up the new subdirectory site
- Copy the WordPress files and database to the new location.
- Update `wp-config.php` with the new database details.
- Set the site URLs to the new subdirectory URL, for example:

```php
define('WP_SITEURL', 'http://www.example.com/blog');
define('WP_HOME', 'http://www.example.com/blog');
```

- Update internal links and media URLs in the database so they point to the new subdirectory.

2. Keep the old subdomain live temporarily
- Do not delete the old subdomain immediately.
- It must remain accessible so it can issue redirects.

3. Add 301 redirects on the old subdomain
- Redirect every request on the old subdomain to the equivalent page in the new subdirectory.
- Example Apache rule:

```apache
Redirect 301 / http://www.example.com/blog/
```

This is the important SEO step: it tells search engines that the old URLs have permanently moved.

4. Verify page-to-page matching
- Best practice is to redirect each old page to its closest equivalent new page, not just everything to the new home page.
- If the old subdomain had specific URLs, map them individually if possible.

5. Update supporting items
- Change canonical tags if used.
- Update XML sitemaps and submit the new sitemap in Search Console.
- Update internal links, feeds, and any external services like FeedBurner if applicable.

6. After Google reindexes
- Keep the redirects in place long-term.
- Do not remove the old subdomain redirect too soon, or you may lose ranking signals.

Important note:
The 301 redirect is what transfers most of the SEO value. Without it, search engines treat the new subdirectory as a separate site.

```html
<script type="application/ld+json">
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "WebSite",
  "url": "https://www.example.com/",
  "potentialAction": {
    "@type": "SearchAction",
    "target": "https://www.example.com/search?q={search_term_string}",
    "query-input": "required name=search_term_string"
  }
}
</script>
```

However, even with this in place, Google may still choose not to display the box.

For SEO, the best approach is usually:

- Set the alternate domains to 301 redirect to your primary domain.

Why:
- Alias-only setups can let the same content be accessed at multiple URLs, which can create duplicate content issues.
- Rewriting content to look like separate domains still leaves you with essentially the same duplicate-content problem.
- Making landing pages with thin or slightly different content usually won’t add real SEO value, and the links won’t be very useful.

So the simplest and best SEO strategy is:
1. Pick one primary domain.
2. 301 redirect all other domains to it.
3. Make sure internal links and canonical URLs point to the primary domain.

That way search engines understand which domain is the main one, and any value from links to the alternate domains gets passed on to the primary site.

Short answer: yes, the domain suffix can matter a little, but it’s not the main SEO factor.

A few key points:

1. Country-code domains signal location
- Domains like .it, .co.uk, .de are country-code top-level domains (ccTLDs).
- Search engines often treat them as a strong signal that the site is intended for users in that country.
- So .it may naturally be associated more with Italy than with the UK or US.

2. That does not mean it ranks worse everywhere
- A .it domain can still rank globally if the content is relevant and strong.
- Search engines do not automatically “penalize” it just because it’s Italian.
- Ranking depends on many factors: content quality, backlinks, site structure, technical SEO, user signals, and relevance.

3. Search results are not limited by the suffix
- Google does not have separate “.co.uk Google” or “.com Google” in the way people sometimes imagine.
- Search results are personalized by location, language, and country settings, not just by the domain ending.
- Google will usually try to show the most relevant results for the user’s region and language.

4. Brand name in the domain can help, but only modestly
- Having the company name in the domain can help with branding and recognition.
- It’s not a major ranking boost by itself.
- Exact-match domains used to matter more, but today content and authority matter much more.

5. If you want to target multiple countries
- Use a generic domain like .com or .net if you want a more neutral international presence.
- If using .it, you can still target other countries with:
  - language-specific content
  - hreflang tags
  - country-specific pages
  - Google Search Console geo-targeting for some domain types

Bottom line:
- SEO is not driven solely by content, but content is a major part.
- A .it domain suggests Italy, but it does not automatically hurt ranking in other countries.
- The biggest factor is still relevance and quality for the searcher.

Google does not guarantee that it will index every page on your site, even if those pages are in your XML sitemap. A sitemap helps Google discover pages, but it does not force indexing.

A few common reasons only part of a site gets indexed:

- Google thinks some pages are low-value, duplicate, thin, or not especially relevant
- The pages are blocked by robots.txt or a meta robots tag
- The pages have crawl errors or redirect issues
- The pages are too similar to other pages already indexed
- Google has discovered them but chosen not to include them in the index

What to check:
- Set up Google Search Console for the site
- Look at Coverage / Indexing reports for crawl errors, excluded pages, and blocked resources
- Inspect a specific URL to see how Googlebot views it
- Check robots.txt and page-level noindex tags

If the landing page is showing in Analytics under Content but not in the source/medium or organic reports, the issue is usually not with the landing page itself—it’s with how traffic is being attributed.

Common causes and fixes:

1. Verify the Google Analytics tag is on the landing page
- Make sure the GA tracking code is present on the actual landing page, not just the checkout or conversion pages.
- If the PPC redirect goes through a different domain or tracking URL, confirm GA is installed before and after the redirect.

2. Check cross-domain or redirect tracking
- If visitors come through a third-party URL or are redirected across domains, GA can lose the original source and classify visits as direct.
- Set up cross-domain tracking if multiple domains are involved.
- Avoid unnecessary redirects that strip UTM parameters or referrer data.

3. Preserve campaign parameters
- If you are using PPC campaign URLs, ensure UTMs are not being removed by the redirect.
- The final landing URL should keep parameters like:
  - utm_source
  - utm_medium
  - utm_campaign

4. Organic/referral traffic may be blocked or misattributed
- If only PPC is appearing, check whether:
  - Organic traffic is being filtered out by a view filter
  - Referral exclusion settings are too broad
  - Self-referrals are causing attribution issues
  - You’re viewing the wrong property or view

5. Check Google Search Console and indexing
- If the page is not appearing in Google search results, that is separate from Analytics.
- In Google Analytics, you can see visits to the landing page, but for Google search visibility you need:
  - The page indexed in Google
  - No robots.txt block
  - No noindex tag
  - A sitemap submitted in Search Console

6. Landing page report vs source reports
- The landing page report shows which pages started sessions.
- Source/medium reports show where the session came from.
- If source data is missing, the session may be getting assigned to direct because referrer/campaign data is being lost during redirects.

What to do next
- Test the PPC URL and organic URL with Google Tag Assistant or GA DebugView.
- Check whether the redirect preserves the referrer and UTM parameters.
- If multiple domains are used, configure cross-domain tracking.
- Review filters and referral exclusions in the GA view.
- Confirm the page is indexable in Google Search Console if the problem is that it is not appearing in Google search, not just Analytics.

Google does not publish a complete list or fixed rule for which synonyms get bolded. In general, it depends on how confident Google is that a term in the result matches the meaning of your query, not just the exact spelling.

- It may bold:

  - stemming variants, like picture/pictures
  - close synonyms or related terms, when it is highly confident they mean the same thing in that context
- It may not bold a synonym consistently if:
  - the word is ambiguous
  - context is weak
  - the result is only partially related
  - another word in the query changes the meaning

Example:
- Search: Japanese cars
- Google might bold car, cars, vehicles, auto, etc. depending on context and the result page.
- But if the page uses a word that could mean something else, Google may not bold it even if it seems related.

Can you find Google’s synonym list?
- No, not directly.
- Google does not expose a public “synonym dictionary” for search.
- The best you can do is observe results and use Google’s search tools or documentation about how search matches terms.

So the short answer is:
- There is no public rule or synonym list.
- Bolding is context-dependent and based on Google’s confidence in semantic equivalence.

- Thin content

- Low-value pages
- Canonical issues
- Crawlable, but not index-worthy
- Noindex tags or blocked resources
- Soft 404s or pages with errors

In short: the sitemap helps Google find pages, but Google only indexes pages it thinks deserve to be indexed.

Yes — use a robots meta tag with `noindex, follow` on the page you want crawled but not shown in Google results:

```html
<meta name="robots" content="noindex, follow" />
```

What this does:
- `noindex` tells Google not to include the page in search results
- `follow` tells Google it can still crawl the links on that page

A couple of notes:
- Put it in the `<head>` section of the page.
- If you want to block all search engines, you can also use `X-Robots-Tag` in HTTP headers.
- Don’t use `robots.txt` alone if you still want Google to access the page and follow links, because blocking via robots.txt can prevent crawling entirely.

If you want, I can also show how to do this in HTML, Apache, Nginx, or WordPress.

If your goal is to keep a page out of Google’s index, the safest approaches are:

1. Use `noindex`
   - Add a meta tag in the page HTML:
     `<meta name="robots" content="noindex">`
   - Or send an HTTP header:
     `X-Robots-Tag: noindex`

2. Block it with `robots.txt`
   - This can prevent crawling, but it does not guarantee de-indexing if the URL is already known or linked elsewhere.
   - Also, Google may still show the URL without content if it learns about it from other sources.

3. Protect it with authentication
   - If the page should not be public, require login or access control.
   - This is the only reliable way to keep content truly hidden.

Important note:
- “Not linked anywhere” does not guarantee Google won’t find it. URLs can be discovered through internal links, sitemaps, logs, referrers, external links, or other pages in the site.
- A “secret” URL is not a security measure.

So:
- If you want it hidden from search results: use `noindex`.

If Googlebot is crawling your site almost 24/7, then yes, your server has to stay available to serve those requests, just like for any other visitor. But “pay per hour” cloud hosting does not mean “only pay when someone visits.”

- Google crawling does add load, but it normally does not make a site “full price monthly” by itself unless your plan is based on always-on infrastructure anyway.

What’s the point of hourly cloud hosting then?

- Flexibility: You can scale up/down or shut down resources when not needed.
- Better fit for variable traffic: Useful for dev/test environments, temporary sites, or workloads that don’t need 24/7 capacity.
- Granular billing: Some cloud services charge only while a VM/container/database is running.
- Control and scalability: You can optimize cost by using smaller instances, autoscaling, caching, CDN, etc.

If your site is public and always online, you will usually still pay for always-on hosting. The benefit of cloud is that you can pay for exactly the resources you use, and scale them, rather than buying a fixed monthly hosting package.

Google does not crawl your database directly. It only crawls URLs it can discover and request over HTTP.

So in your setup:

- `home.php` can be indexed if Google finds it.
- `articles.php` can be indexed if Google can reach it via a normal link.
- `display.php?id=1`, `display.php?id=2`, etc. can each be indexed as separate pages if:
  - they are linked from crawlable HTML links, and
  - they return unique, accessible content.

Important points:

1. You do not need a separate physical file for each article
   One PHP script like `display.php` can serve many article pages from the database.

2. Google indexes URLs, not your database rows
   If each article has its own URL, Google can index them.

3. Your article links must be crawlable
   Use regular `<a href="...">` links, not links that only appear after JavaScript clicks or form actions.

4. Each article page should have unique content and metadata
   Different title tags, meta descriptions, headings, and body content help Google understand each page.

5. If only the home page is showing up, common causes are:
   - the other pages are not linked properly
   - they are blocked by robots.txt or meta noindex
   - Google has not discovered them yet
   - the pages return duplicate/thin content
   - the pages require JavaScript or a login to view

So yes, Google can recognize your articles if each one has its own reachable URL like:

- `www.example.com/articlenew/display.php?id=1`
- `www.example.com/articlenew/display.php?id=2`

As long as those URLs are accessible and linked properly, Google can crawl and index them.

Because a `site:example.com` search is not a reliable “all indexed pages” report.

In the resolved thread, the key point was:

- The home page is already indexed and cached by Google.
- `site:` results are incomplete and can be inconsistent.
- The fact that other pages appear above the home page does not mean the home page is missing or penalized.

Why this happens:
- Google does not guarantee that `site:domain.com` shows every indexed URL.
- Results from `site:` queries are often ranked strangely.
- Sometimes the homepage is omitted from that view even though it is indexed.
- The homepage may also be canonicalized to another URL, such as:
  - `https://example.com/`
  - `https://www.example.com/`
  - `/index.html`
  - `/index.php`

What to check:
1. Search for the homepage title or a unique sentence from the homepage.
2. Use Google Search Console’s URL Inspection tool on the homepage.
3. Make sure only one preferred version is used:
   - www or non-www
   - http or https
4. Check that the homepage has:
   - a 200 status code
   - no `noindex`
   - a correct canonical tag
   - no redirect loops or conflicting rewrite rules

About your `.htaccess`:
- The `RewriteRule ^index\.php$ / [QSA,R=301]` is fine if you want `/index.php` to redirect to `/`.
- But if the homepage is accessible through multiple versions, Google may treat one as canonical and show another in results.

So the short answer is:  
Your homepage is probably indexed already; `site:` just isn’t showing it. Check the URL directly in Search Console and verify canonical/redirect consistency.

A likely cause is that the pages/sections are being rendered differently by Internet Explorer because of compatibility mode, not because of IIS itself.

- IE can force intranet sites into Compatibility View by default.
- That can make the same page render slightly differently across servers/environments.
- Even if your HTML/web.config says to use IE=edge, the browser can still override it.
- Firefox may appear fine because it isn’t using the same compatibility behavior.

How this relates to “specific site sections with significantly low appearance in SERP”:
- If those sections are visible/structured differently on the live site due to browser rendering issues, search engines may also see different DOM/CSS behavior depending on how the page is served or tested.
- More commonly, though, low SERP appearance for only some sections is usually caused by indexing/rendering issues such as:
  - content loaded via JavaScript that isn’t crawlable
  - hidden/duplicated content
  - canonical or noindex issues
  - poor internal linking to those sections
  - thin/low-value content
  - broken HTML/CSS affecting renderability
  - mobile/desktop rendering differences

3. Compare crawlable content vs what users see.
4. Check for:

   - robots.txt blocks
   - JS-inserted content
   - misplaced headings/links
5. In IE specifically, verify Compatibility View settings if you’re seeing rendering anomalies.

So the thread’s core lesson is: small rendering differences can be caused by browser compatibility mode, especially in IE, and those differences can lead to broken layouts or inconsistent visibility. Yes — hidden content can be a factor, but usually not because Google “punishes” the mere presence of `display:none` divs. The main issue is whether the hidden sections are:

1. important content you want indexed, or
2. a lot of duplicate / low-value markup that can dilute the page’s visible signal.

In your case, if every non-logged page contains the same hidden login/signup blocks before the main content, that usually won’t directly cause a penalty. Google can render JavaScript and understand hidden elements, but it also evaluates whether the page is trying to present different content to users vs. bots.

What to watch for:
- If the hidden divs contain substantial text, keywords, or repeated content, they may reduce the clarity of the page’s main topic.
- If the content is hidden only for UX reasons and then shown on user interaction, that’s generally fine.
- If the hidden content is very large, duplicated across many pages, or looks like “keyword stuffing,” that can hurt.

Why a specific site section might have low SERP appearance:
- The section may have weak internal linking
- The section content may be too similar to other pages
- The section may be buried behind JS or hidden by default
- The page may have indexing/canonical issues
- The section may have low content quality or poor relevance signals

Best practice:
- Keep login/signup UI in the HTML if needed, but don’t load it with lots of keyword-rich text.
- Make sure the main content is visible and accessible immediately.
- If the hidden forms are large, consider moving them lower in the DOM or loading them only when needed.
- Ensure the important site sections are linked clearly from crawlable navigation.
- Use Google Search Console to inspect the affected URLs and see if they’re being rendered/indexed as expected.

So: hidden divs are not automatically bad for SEO, but they can contribute to lower visibility if they add clutter, duplicate content, or obscure the real page focus. If you want, I can help you audit whether your specific hidden sections are likely causing the SERP problem.

For OpenCart product pages, the main SEO goal is to make each important product page indexable, unique, and easy for Google to understand.

1. Use clean, readable URLs
   - Good:
     /product/brand/model
     /cars/audi/a4
   - Avoid messy query strings for primary pages if possible:
     ?brand=audi&model=a4

2. Make sure each product has a unique page
   - Unique title tag
   - Unique H1
   - Unique description content
   - Unique images and alt text
   - Structured data if possible

3. Use canonical URLs correctly
   - If the same product can be reached through multiple URLs, set one preferred canonical URL.
   - Example:
     /product/audi/a4 and /cars/audi/a4?sort=price
     both canonicalize to:
     /cars/audi/a4
   - Canonical is useful for duplicates, not for every different product page.

4. Handle filters carefully
   - Faceted/filter pages can create lots of duplicate or thin pages.
   - If filter combinations don’t have search value, noindex them.
   - If a filter combination is important, create a static SEO landing page for it.
   - Example:
     /cars/audi/suv
     /cars/bmw/sedan

5. Pagination
   - Paginated pages should remain crawlable.
   - Use self-referencing canonicals on paginated pages, not all to page 1.
   - Example:
     /cars?page=2 canonical to itself

6. Create SEO landing pages for important categories
   - Brand pages
   - Model pages
   - Popular filter combinations
   - These can be static or semi-static and linked from category/navigation pages.

7. Internal linking
   - Link products from category pages, breadcrumbs, and related products.
   - Breadcrumbs help both users and search engines.

8. OpenCart-specific tips
   - Enable SEO-friendly URLs.
   - Use an SEO extension if needed for better control of URL aliases, canonical tags, and pagination.
   - Make sure XML sitemaps include only canonical, indexable URLs.

Short answer:
- Use clean, static, crawlable URLs for important pages.
- Canonicalize duplicates.
- Noindex weak filter pages.
- Create SEO landing pages for high-value brand/model/filter combinations.

- fast, accessible pages

Yes, this can be expected right after a 301 migration.

What’s likely happening:

- Google already knows your old domain and is still treating it as the source of the indexed URLs.
- After a 301 redirect, Google needs time to recrawl the old URLs, see the redirects, and transfer signals/indexing to the new domain.
- In Google Webmaster Tools/Search Console, the old property may still show the sitemap and indexed data while the new property temporarily shows 0 pages.

What to do:

1. Use the Change of Address tool in Google Webmaster Tools/Search Console  
   - This tells Google that the site has permanently moved.
   - Link: https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/83106?hl=en

2. Submit your sitemap for the old site again  
   - This helps Google discover the 301 redirects from the old URLs to the new ones.

3. Submit the sitemap for the new site  
   - This helps Google crawl and index the new URLs directly.

4. Check visibility with a site: search  
   - Example: `site:www.mysite.com`
   - This is often more telling than Search Console data early on.

A few important notes:

- It can take days or weeks for Google to fully process a domain move.
- A 0 indexed pages report in the new property right after the redirect does not necessarily mean something is wrong.
- Make sure the new site is crawlable and not blocked by robots.txt, meta noindex, or canonical tags pointing back to the old domain.

So yes: this is normal during a 301 migration, and the key steps are the Change of Address request plus sitemap submission for both domains.

This sounds like a DNS cache/propagation issue, not a WordPress Multisite problem.

If `feeds.mydomain.com` is already set as a CNAME to Feedburner’s server, but visiting it still shows WordPress trying to create a new site, then one of these is usually happening:

- your local machine/browser is still using cached DNS
- your router or ISP DNS cache has not refreshed yet
- the CNAME is not fully propagated everywhere
- WordPress is catching the request because the subdomain still resolves to your server for some clients

What to try:

1. Test from another device or network  
   - Use a different computer, phone on mobile data, or an online DNS checker.
   - If it works elsewhere, that confirms cache/propagation.

2. Flush local DNS cache  
   - Windows: `ipconfig /flushdns`
   - macOS: flush DNS cache depending on version
   - Also try a different browser or incognito mode

3. Verify the DNS record  
   - Make sure `feeds.mydomain.com` is a CNAME pointing exactly to the Feedburner hostname they gave you.
   - Ensure there isn’t also an A record for the same subdomain.

4. Wait for propagation  
   - DNS changes can take time depending on TTL and caching.

For SEO, the main thing to distinguish is:

- `alt` attribute on images
- `title` attribute on elements
- `<title>` element of the page

They have different purposes and different practical limits.

### 1) `alt` attribute
There is no hard maximum length, but best practice is to keep it concise and descriptive. For accessibility, many recommend staying around 125 characters or less.

A 200-word `alt` text is usually too long. It may be ignored by assistive tech users, and it looks like keyword stuffing to search engines.

Use `alt` for:
- what the image shows
- short functional descriptions if the image is a link/button

If you need a long explanation, put that in nearby body text or in a caption, not in `alt`.

### 2) `title` attribute
Again, no strict maximum, but it’s not meant for long text. Browsers often show it as a tooltip, and long text may be cut off or awkward to use.

So keep it short and helpful.

### 3) `<title>` element
If you mean the page title in HTML, then yes, length matters for SEO. Search engines may truncate it or rewrite it.

A common recommendation is:
- keep it under about 60–70 characters
- make it unique and relevant
- avoid stuffing in too many keyphrases

### About SEO and autosuggestions
If you’re asking whether search engines “like” long alt text or keyword-heavy text: generally, no. They prefer natural, helpful descriptions. Overly long or repetitive text can look spammy and is not a good SEO strategy.

### Practical advice
- Use short, accurate `alt` text
- Use `title` sparingly
- Put detailed text in visible page content instead
- For page titles, stay concise and readable

This is usually not a sign that your pages aren’t indexed. It’s more often a reporting delay or a mismatch between what Webmaster Tools/Search Console is counting in each report.

A few common reasons:

1. Different reports update at different times
- The Sitemap report and Index Status report are not always in sync.
- Google can already have your pages in search results, while the sitemap processing/reporting still shows 0 or only 1 indexed.

2. “Indexed” in the sitemap report is not a direct live count
- In the Sitemap section, Google is comparing submitted URLs to URLs it has associated with that sitemap.
- If Google hasn’t yet crawled the sitemap URLs recently, or hasn’t matched them back to the sitemap, it may show 0 indexed.

3. Search results you see may be from cached/known URLs
- When you search for your site and see pages, that doesn’t always mean the reports have fully caught up.
- Google may show them in results while the reporting system still lags behind.

4. Canonical/duplicate URL differences
- If the same page is accessible via multiple URLs, Search Console may count them differently.
- Example: `http://`, `https://`, `www`, non-`www`, trailing slash vs no trailing slash.
- The sitemap may list one version, while Google indexes another canonical version.

5. New or small sites often show inconsistent counts
- For small sites, the numbers can look odd because a few pages make a big percentage change.
- It’s common to see temporary mismatches like “6 submitted, 0 indexed” or “11 indexed” in another report.

What to check:
- Make sure the sitemap URLs exactly match the preferred canonical URLs.
- Check that each page has a self-referencing canonical tag if appropriate.
- Ensure there are no `noindex` tags, robots.txt blocks, or redirects on the submitted URLs.
- Give it time: reprocessing can take days or even weeks.

Bottom line:
If your pages are appearing in Google search, they are likely indexed. The “0 indexed” in the sitemap report is often just a reporting inconsistency or delay, not a real problem.

Example:

- If you choose no trailing slashes: redirect `/page/5/` → `/page/5`

To remove trailing slashes with `.htaccess`, you can redirect any URL that ends in `/` to the same URL without it.

Example:

```apache
RewriteEngine On

# Remove trailing slash except for real directories/files
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-d
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-f
RewriteRule ^(.+?)/$ /$1 [R=301,L]
```

If you want the opposite behavior, to always add a trailing slash, use:

```apache
RewriteEngine On

# Add trailing slash except for real files/directories
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-d
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-f
RewriteRule ^(.+[^/])$ /$1/ [R=301,L]
```

SEO-wise, the important part is consistency. `/page/5` and `/page/5/` are treated as different URLs, so pick one version and redirect the other to it with a 301 redirect to avoid duplicate content.

Yes — in this situation you should block the site search/results URLs from Googlebot with robots.txt, while still allowing crawl access to your actual content pages.

Key points:

- Don’t let Google crawl internal search results pages.
  - Google generally does not want to index site-search pages.
  - Crawling them can waste a lot of crawl budget.
  - It can also create spam/quality risks if arbitrary queries produce indexable pages.

- `noindex` alone is not enough if Google is spending huge crawl resources on the pages.
  - `noindex` can keep them out of the index, but Google still has to crawl them to see the tag.
  - If your main issue is 200k bot search requests/day, robots.txt is the better fix.

- A sitemap is helpful, but it does not replace crawlability.
  - A sitemap can help Google discover your real content pages.
  - But if pages are blocked from crawling or otherwise unreachable, a sitemap won’t “fix” that.
  - So use the sitemap to support discovery, not as a substitute for internal linking/crawl access.

Recommended approach:

1. Add `Disallow` rules in robots.txt for your internal search URLs.
   Example:
   `Disallow: /search`
   or whatever your search path/query patterns are.

2. Keep content pages crawlable.
   - Don’t block the actual article/product/detail URLs.
   - Make sure Google can reach them through normal links.

3. Submit a sitemap of real content pages.
   - This helps discovery and indexing of your important pages.

4. Remove `rel=next/prev` if it’s only for search results pages.
   - Those hints don’t solve the core issue here.

5. Make sure important content is discoverable in a few clicks.
   - Good internal linking matters more than search-result crawling.

Bottom line: blocking site search in robots.txt should reduce Googlebot load without harming rankings, as long as your real content remains crawlable and well-linked.

   - If you’re on Nginx, add redirect rules in the site config.

3. Group redirects where possible  
   - If many old URLs follow a pattern, redirect whole folders or sections instead of individual pages.
   - Example:
     - `/news_article/01` -> `/news/01/`
     - `/news_article/02` -> `/news/02/`

     - `/news_article/` -> `/news/`

4. Handle pages and images separately  
   - Old image links also need redirects if they’re still indexed or linked externally.

Example Apache rules:

```apache

Redirect permanent /news_article/02 http://www.mydomain.com/news/02/
Redirect permanent /news_article http://www.mydomain.com/news/
```

- create a redirect map,

Yes — if you’re moving back to the old pages, the right approach is to 301 redirect the current/new URLs back to the old URLs.

Key points:

- Do not keep both sets of redirects active in both directions.
- If you redirect old URLs to new URLs, and then new URLs back to old URLs, you’ll create redirect loops.
- Since the new URLs are likely the ones currently indexed by search engines, you want:
  - new site URLs -> old site URLs via 301
  - and remove the old -> new redirects if the old pages are going to exist again

Best practice:
1. Restore the old pages/content if possible.
2. Set 301 redirects from every current/new URL to its matching old URL.
3. Update your XML sitemap to list the old URLs.
4. Make sure internal links point to the old URLs, not the redirected ones.
5. Submit the updated sitemap in Search Console / Webmaster Tools.

SEO impact:
- A 301 redirect passes most link equity.
- Rankings may fluctuate for a while after the switch.
- If the rollback is clean and the old pages truly come back, search engines can eventually recover previous rankings.
- Avoid chains and loops as much as possible.

Use a 301 redirect in the old site’s `.htaccess` so every request goes to the new domain, preserving the path and query string.

Example:

```apache
RewriteEngine On
RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} !^www\.newdomain\.com$ [NC]
RewriteRule ^(.*)$ https://www.newdomain.com%{REQUEST_URI} [R=301,L]
```

What this does:
- redirects `old-domain.com/anything`
- redirects `www.old-domain.com/folder/page`
- redirects any other host serving that same content
- sends users to the same path on `www.newdomain.com`

If you want to redirect both the root domain and any subdomains, this simpler version is often enough:

```apache
RewriteEngine On
RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} !^www\.newdomain\.com$ [NC]
RewriteRule ^ https://www.newdomain.com%{REQUEST_URI} [R=301,L]
```

Notes:
- Put this in the `.htaccess` on the old site / old domain.
- Make sure `mod_rewrite` is enabled.
- If the new site uses `http` instead of `https`, change the target URL accordingly.

Search engines can crawl and index PDF files pretty well, but a few things matter:

1. They need to be able to fetch the PDF directly
   - A URL like /files/doc.pdf is easy for Google to recognize and index.
   - If you serve the same PDF through a PHP download script with:
     - Content-Type: application/octet-stream
     - Content-Disposition: attachment
     
     then many crawlers will treat it as a generic downloadable file, not as a PDF document.

2. The MIME type matters
   - For PDF, the correct header is:
     Content-Type: application/pdf
   - If you send application/octet-stream, you’re basically saying “generic binary file,” which is less SEO-friendly and may prevent proper PDF handling.

3. The URL shape matters too
   - Search engines often use the URL extension as a clue.
   - A URL ending in .pdf is much more likely to be recognized as a PDF than something like /pdf.php?id=1.

4. Attachment vs inline delivery
   - If you force download with Content-Disposition: attachment, the browser downloads it instead of displaying it.
   - Search engines may still fetch it, but this is less ideal for indexing and document understanding than serving it inline.

Best practice for SEO:
- Serve PDFs as direct URLs with a .pdf extension if possible.
- Use Content-Type: application/pdf.
- Avoid forcing attachment unless you really want the file downloaded rather than viewed.
- Make sure the PDFs are linked from crawlable pages and included in your sitemap if relevant.

So yes, from an SEO point of view, serving PDFs as static files is generally better than hiding them behind a download script. If you must use PHP, make the URL and headers look like a real PDF resource.

The key idea is:

4. Preserve ecommerce tracking

Google controls sitelinks, not you.

If your site shows sitelinks for `word1 word2` but not for `word1word2`, it’s likely because Google is interpreting the unspaced version differently — even if that’s your exact brand name. There isn’t a guaranteed way to force sitelinks for that query.

What you can do is only “encourage” them:

- Make sure your site structure is clear and easy to crawl
- Use consistent brand naming across the site and external profiles
- Ensure good internal linking to important pages
- Submit a clean sitemap in Google Search Console
- Build strong brand signals around the exact name

But even with all that, Google may still choose not to show sitelinks for the concatenated version.

The search box under a site’s Google result is not something you can directly turn on yourself. It’s generated by Google at its discretion.

What you can do:
- Make sure your site has strong, indexable internal search functionality.
- Consider setting up Google’s Custom Search Engine (CSE) or a comparable site search, since that may increase the chance Google shows the box.
- Ensure your site structure is clear and your pages are easy for Google to crawl.

But even with all that, Google may still choose to show only sitelinks and no search box. There’s no guaranteed way to force it.

Google decides this automatically.

There isn’t a public set of rules or a manual setting that lets you choose whether sitelinks appear with a search bar or not. In general:

- Google shows sitelinks based on its own assessment of the site.
- The search bar is also added or omitted by Google automatically.
- Having a solid internal site search function likely helps, but there’s no guarantee.

So the short answer is: you can’t control it directly; Google determines whether the search bar is shown.

When choosing a scalable eCommerce platform for a medium-sized company, focus less on “hiding” the technology and more on whether the platform is a good fit operationally and technically.

A practical way to evaluate platforms:

1. Scalability and performance
- Can it handle current traffic and growth?
- Check limits on products, orders, users, API calls, and catalog complexity.
- Ask about CDN support, caching, multi-region support, and peak-load behavior.

2. Total cost of ownership
- Include licensing, hosting, transaction fees, extensions, development, maintenance, and upgrades.
- Some platforms look cheap up front but become expensive as you scale.

3. Flexibility and integrations
- Make sure it integrates with your ERP, CRM, payment gateways, shipping, tax, analytics, and marketing tools.
- Verify API quality and webhook/event support.

4. Security and compliance
- Look for PCI compliance, SSO, role-based access, audit logging, and regular patching.
- This is usually more important than obscuring which platform you use.

5. Admin usability and team fit
- Your operations, marketing, and support teams should be able to manage products, promotions, and orders without heavy developer involvement.

6. Ecosystem and support
- Consider the vendor’s support quality, partner network, app marketplace, and documentation.
- A mature ecosystem can save a lot of implementation time.

7. Migration and long-term lock-in
- Check how easy it is to export products, customers, orders, and content later.
- Medium-sized companies often outgrow rigid platforms or get stuck with one vendor.

- Shopify Plus: strong for speed, managed hosting, ease of use
- Magento/Adobe Commerce: highly flexible, more complex to run
- BigCommerce: good middle ground for SaaS + flexibility
- Salesforce Commerce Cloud: strong enterprise ecosystem, often higher cost
- Headless setups (for example, commercetools + frontend framework): very scalable, but more engineering-heavy

A good selection process:
- Define your 3-year growth targets
- List required integrations and custom features
- Shortlist 3 platforms
- Run a proof of concept with real catalog/order workflows
- Estimate implementation and ongoing support costs

If your concern is discovery or “being identifiable” on the web, note that technologies are often discoverable through page content, cookies, headers, or known paths. In practice, it’s usually better to keep the platform secure and updated than to focus on hiding it. The important question is whether the platform meets your business and technical needs.

For a medium-sized company, the main question isn’t “which platform is best overall?” but “which platform best matches your current and near-future complexity?”

A good way to identify a scalable eCommerce platform is to evaluate these areas:

1. Product and catalog complexity
- Number of SKUs now and in 12–24 months
- Variants, bundles, subscriptions, and custom pricing
- Need for categories, tags, search, and filters
- Multiple languages or multiple currencies

2. Market and payment needs
- Which countries you sell to
- Required payment methods by region
- Need for local gateways, cards, wallets, bank transfer, COD, etc.
- Tax rules and compliance requirements

3. Operational complexity
- Inventory management across one or many warehouses
- Shipping rules, carriers, fulfillment integrations
- Returns, refunds, promotions, and discount logic
- ERP, CRM, accounting, and POS integrations

4. Scalability and flexibility
- Can the platform handle traffic spikes and growth?
- Can it support more products, more regions, and more transactions without a rebuild?
- API quality and extensibility
- Theme/customization limits versus development effort

5. Total cost of ownership
- Monthly fees, transaction fees, app/plugin costs
- Development and maintenance effort
- Hosting and security if self-hosted
- Cost of future migration if you outgrow it

6. Ownership and control
- Hosted SaaS platform: faster to launch, less maintenance, less control
- Self-hosted/open-source: more control, more flexibility, more maintenance

Practical rule of thumb
- Use a hosted platform like Shopify if you want speed, reliability, and standard workflows.
- Use a more customizable platform like Magento/Adobe Commerce, WooCommerce, or a headless setup if you need deeper customization or complex business logic.
- Avoid building from scratch unless your requirements are highly unique and you have the team to maintain it long-term.

How to decide
Create a shortlist and score each platform against:
- Your must-have features
- Growth ceiling
- Integration support
- Regional payment support
- Maintenance burden
- 3-year cost

Yes, but the best method depends on what you mean by “Apache serving requests for content from other sites.”

A few important points:

- Apache itself does not normally “connect to a domain” unless a script or module running under it does that.
- If the PHP script is making the outbound request, the fix is usually at the PHP/application or firewall level, not Apache.

Options:

1. Block the domain at the network level
- Use a firewall rule to block outbound connections to that site’s IP.
- Example idea:
  - iptables -A OUTPUT -d <IP_OF_SOMESITE> -j DROP
- If the domain has multiple IPs or changes often, this can be tricky.

2. Stop the PHP script from making the request
- If you control the script, add logic to prevent requests to that domain.
- This is usually the cleanest solution.

3. Rewrite or redirect the incoming URL
- If the issue is that users can pass the target site in the URL, you can use Apache rewrite rules or .htaccess to reject or redirect those requests.

4. Disable external fetching in PHP
- Depending on what the script uses, you may be able to restrict:
  - allow_url_fopen
  - cURL outbound behavior
  - proxy settings
- But this is more about PHP configuration than Apache.

If you want to block Apache/PHP from reaching specific external sites, firewall rules or application changes are the right approach. Apache alone does not have a simple built-in “block this remote domain” feature.

If you want, I can give you:
- an iptables example,
- an Apache .htaccess rule,
- or a PHP code snippet to block the domain.

Yes, you can drop them before Apache sees them, but the best place depends on what you can reliably match.

Best options, in order:

1. Drop at the edge router/firewall
   - If the traffic has a recognizable signature, block it at the external router or upstream firewall.
   - This is the most efficient place because the packets never reach your server.

2. Use a firewall with smarter inspection
   - If you have an inboard firewall that supports deep packet inspection or application-aware rules, translate your Apache deny rules there.
   - This reduces load before traffic gets to Apache.

3. Use iptables/nftables on the host
   - This can drop packets before they hit Apache, but it’s not very intelligent.
   - It works best if you can match on source IPs, ports, connection patterns, or other simple signatures.

4. As a last resort, suppress logging in Apache
   - You can avoid logging specific denied requests, but this is usually not recommended.
   - Logs are useful if you later need to analyze attack patterns or changes.

So, yes, iptables is one way, but ideally you block at the router or firewall upstream of Apache. If the requests are all from many different IPs and vary a lot, you may need a more intelligent firewall rule set or rate-limiting/protection tool rather than simple IP blocking.

What’s probably happening is:

- In that cached copy, Google sees a bad link such as `www.example.com/shop/=` or similar.
- Google then reports the 404 based on the old cached content, even though your live page no longer contains that link.

That would also explain why:

- you can’t find the link in the current HTML,
- your crawler doesn’t report it,
- fetching as Google doesn’t reproduce it,
- only deeper pages like `/shop/gift-voucher` show the issue.

What you can do:

1. Re-fetch the affected pages in Google Search Console / Webmaster Tools  
   This refreshes Google’s cached copy and may stop it from following the stale bad link.

2. Add a redirect or rewrite rule for the bad URL pattern  
   If Google keeps hitting the broken URL, redirect it to the correct page or parent section so it doesn’t get a 404.

3. Check for generated links in templates, JavaScript, or cached output  
   Even if the source looks clean now, the bad link may have existed previously in:
   - an old template,
   - cached HTML,
   - server-side generated content,
   - a CMS module.

4. Wait and monitor  
   If the bad link has already been fixed, the 404 reports may gradually disappear as Google recrawls and refreshes its cache.

So in short: yes, Google may be “doing its own thing” by following an outdated cached version of the page. The most practical fix is to refresh the pages in Search Console and/or redirect the bad URL.

Yes — the key point is that Apache/PHP cannot send a real 404/410 after output has already started, because HTTP status must be sent in headers before any body content.

So if the page starts rendering and only later the code discovers “this content doesn’t exist,” it’s too late to correctly change the status code. The fix is to check whether the content exists first, then either:

- send a 404/410 header and the error page, or
- generate the normal page

In PHP, that means something like:

```php
if (!$content_exists) {
    header("HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found");
    include "404.php";
    exit;
}
```

A few important notes:

- A redirect to a 404 page is not the same as returning a 404.
- If your current setup uses a 301 or 302 redirect to `/404.php`, that is not ideal for missing content.
- Redirects are also headers, so if a redirect can be sent, a 404 could have been sent too.

Best practice:
- Use a true 404 for content that never existed or is missing.
- Use a 410 Gone if the content used to exist but has been permanently removed.

If this is an Apache/site architecture issue, the clean solution is to make sure the existence check happens before any HTML output begins. If that’s not practical, you can still use Apache’s error handling to serve a custom 404 page, but the response code should remain 404, not 302/301.

So: redirecting users to a 404 page is common, but it’s not the same as properly serving a 404 status. For SEO and correctness, returning the actual 404/410 is better.

You can do this with a rewrite rule, so the browser shows a nice URL like:

website.com/profile/kevinlee

while your server actually loads something like:

profile.php?username=kevinlee

A simple Apache .htaccess example:

```apache
Options +FollowSymLinks
RewriteEngine On

RewriteRule ^profile/([^/]+)/?$ profile.php?username=$1 [L,QSA]
```

What this does:
- `^profile/` matches URLs starting with `/profile/`
- `([^/]+)` captures the username part
- `/?$` makes the trailing slash optional
- `profile.php?username=$1` sends the captured username to your PHP script

Example:
- `website.com/profile/kevinlee`
- rewrites to `website.com/profile.php?username=kevinlee`

Then in `profile.php`, you can read it with:

```php
$username = $_GET['username'];
```

A couple of notes:
- Usernames should be unique if you want this style of URL.
- Make sure `mod_rewrite` is enabled on Apache.
- You may need to adjust your existing `/profile/` setup if there’s an `index.php` there already.

Short answer: yes, it’s technically possible, but it’s generally a bad idea for SEO.

Why:
- Search engines may see the same content on two different domains and treat it as duplicate content.
- This can split ranking signals between the domains.
- It can also confuse users and browsers if links, forms, cookies, or scripts expect the real host.

If your goal is to keep one “main” domain visible while serving content from another, the better approaches are:

1. 301 redirect to the preferred domain
   - Best for SEO.
   - Tells search engines the canonical location.
   - The browser URL changes to the destination domain.

2. Canonical tags
   - If duplicate content must exist temporarily, use:
     <link rel="canonical" href="https://domain1.com/path/to/internal/link/" />
   - This tells search engines which version should be indexed.

3. Reverse proxy
   - If you truly need the content to appear under domain1.com while being served from domain2.com, a reverse proxy is the cleaner technical approach than iframe-style masking.
   - Still, you must configure canonical URLs and make sure all generated links/assets are consistent.

Important note:
If you just want to “hide” domain2.com in the address bar while showing its content under domain1.com, that’s not a normal redirect. A redirect changes the URL; masking requires proxying or rewriting.

So the best practice is:
- Use 301 redirects if domain1 and domain2 are the same site.
- Use canonical URLs if both domains must stay accessible.
- Avoid masking/cloaking unless you fully understand the SEO and maintenance downsides.

- a 301 redirect,
- canonical tags,
- or a reverse proxy for Apache/Nginx.

Use hreflang / alternate language markup.

That tells search engines that different URLs are language- or region-specific equivalents of the same content, so they can crawl and index the localized version and show it in the right locale.

- Add `rel="alternate" hreflang="..."` links between them
- Include a self-referencing hreflang tag on each page
- Optionally add the hreflang mappings in your XML sitemap
- Make sure each localized page is crawlable and not hidden behind geo/language redirects

Example:

```html
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="en" href="https://example.com/en/page" />
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="fr" href="https://example.com/fr/page" />
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="de" href="https://example.com/de/page" />
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="x-default" href="https://example.com/" />
```

A few important notes:
- Avoid automatically redirecting search engines or users based only on language detection if you can; Google recommends against that.
- Make sure the content on each localized page is actually localized, not just machine-translated duplicates.
- Keep strong internal linking between the language versions.

- `http://www.example.com/page`

If both versions are reachable and serve the same content, that can create duplicate URL issues. The DNS record type is not the problem.

3. Optionally set your preferred domain in Google Search Console / webmaster tools

So the short answer is: CNAME vs A record does not affect SEO. Duplicate accessible URLs can, but that is solved by redirects or canonicals, not by changing DNS.

  - missing/invalid user agents
- Use caching/CDN/WAF if possible.

You’ll want to use `mod_rewrite` in Apache.

For example, to turn:

`home.php?kategori=dress`

into:

`home.php/dress`

you can add a rewrite rule in your `.htaccess` file like this:

```apache
RewriteEngine On
RewriteRule ^home\.php/([^/]+)/?$ home.php?kategori=$1 [L,QSA]
```

This makes Apache rewrite requests for `home.php/dress` internally to `home.php?kategori=dress`.

- `mod_rewrite` must be enabled on your server.
- `QSA` keeps any existing query string parameters.
- You can adjust the pattern if you want to support more URL parts.

Firefox is warning you because the HTTPS page is loading content over plain HTTP, or because the login flow starts on a non-secure page.

Key point: the whole login process should be on HTTPS.

What’s wrong with the setup described:

- The form is served from `http://.../login.php`
- Even if the form posts to `https://.../post.php`, the login page itself is not protected
- Any scripts, images, or other assets on that page could be intercepted or modified
- If the page is mixed content, Firefox will report non-secure elements

Also, if you redirect back to `http://.../success.php` or `http://.../fail.php`, you lose the protection after login as well.

Recommended setup:

- Serve the login page over HTTPS:
  `https://www.example.com/login.php`
- Post the form to an HTTPS URL:
  `https://somethingelse.example.com/post.php`
- Keep the verification and success/fail pages on HTTPS too
- If you have to redirect, redirect to HTTPS pages, not HTTP

So the secure answer is: yes, the form data sent to an HTTPS action is encrypted in transit, but the overall design is still not secure if the page itself or the return pages are HTTP.

Best practice:
- Use HTTPS for the entire authentication flow
- Optionally redirect all HTTP requests to HTTPS
- Avoid loading any HTTP resources on HTTPS pages

Google usually shows a page/file in search results because it found a link to it somewhere and crawled it.

What likely happened
- The URL was linked from another page, site, or even a test/staging environment.
- Google indexed that URL because it was publicly reachable.
- If the file is in a folder structure, Google does not care about the folder itself unless the URL is accessible and linked somewhere.

How to check where Google found it
- Search your domain with:
  site:yourwebsite.com
- This can help you see what URLs Google has indexed.

How to stop Google from indexing it
1. Use robots.txt
   - Add a robots.txt file at the site root.
   - Block the specific folder or file path.
   - Example:
     User-agent: *
     Disallow: /yourfolder/yourfile.aspx

   Important: robots.txt prevents crawling, but if the URL is already indexed, it may still appear for a while.

2. Use noindex on the page
   - If it’s an HTML page or MVC view, add:
     <meta name="robots" content="noindex, nofollow">
   - Or send an X-Robots-Tag header from ASP.NET if needed.
   - This is better than robots.txt when you want the page crawled but not indexed.

3. Restrict access if it should not be public
   - If the file should only be accessible to certain users or sites, require authentication/authorization.
   - If the URL is truly private, don’t rely only on robots.txt.

4. Remove it from Google faster
   - Use Google Search Console to request removal of the URL.

If you want to block only certain incoming requests
- Use server-side checks in MVC to allow only approved users/sessions/referrers.
- But note: checking the HTTP referrer alone is not secure, because it can be missing or spoofed.

Best practice
- For public pages you do not want indexed: use noindex.
- For private content: require authentication and authorization.
- For old indexed URLs: remove access and request removal in Search Console.

Googlebot is not really “giving value” to useless words in the way you might think. What’s happening is usually one or more of these:

1. Crawl frequency changes
- Google may crawl a page often at first, then less often later.
- New pages sometimes get a temporary boost or “freshness” effect, then settle down.
- So ranking movement in the first weeks is normal.

2. Ranking is based on many signals, not just indexing
- Being indexed with `site:yourpage.com` only means Google knows the page exists.
- It does not mean Google thinks the page is the best result for your keyword.
- If your page is thin, weakly linked, or not clearly focused, it can move around or disappear for that query.

3. “Useless words” can matter if they affect relevance
- Google reads the whole page, including headings, body text, navigation, and sometimes boilerplate text.
- Repeated or irrelevant words can dilute topical focus.
- If your page contains lots of generic text, Google may struggle to understand what the page is really about.

What you should do:
- Make the page clearly about one topic/keyword.
- Remove or reduce irrelevant words, repeated phrases, and boilerplate text.
- Improve title, headings, and main content so they match the search intent.
- Get quality backlinks or internal links from relevant pages.
- Make sure the page has enough unique, useful content.

Important:
- Googlebot crawling more often does not automatically improve rank.
- More crawling is mainly a sign Google is aware of your page.
- Ranking depends on relevance, quality, authority, and user intent.

So the short answer: Google is not “counting useless words” as valuable in a simple way; it is evaluating the entire page and may be finding the page weakly relevant for your keyword. If you want, I can help you audit the page text and show which words or sections are hurting relevance.

If the widget is embedded on other people’s sites, a DIV/embed is generally much better for SEO than an iFrame.

- Content rendered directly in the page DOM via a DIV is more likely to be crawled and counted as part of that page.

- Make sure the widget content is crawlable in plain HTML, not only injected by complex JS after load.

Why:
- An iframe is treated as a separate document. Search engines generally index the iframe source URL, not the embedding page’s content.
- A DIV/inline widget places the content directly in the page’s HTML, so it can be crawled and associated with that page.

Practical guidance:
- Render the widget content server-side or inject it into the DOM as normal HTML.
- Avoid relying only on JavaScript to build the content after load if you want SEO benefits.
- Make sure the text is visible in the page source or rendered HTML that crawlers can access.
- Keep important content accessible without requiring interaction.

So, if you want your customers’ websites to benefit SEO-wise from the widget content, serve it as inline HTML/DIV, not an iframe.

- Anchor text with “best blue widget” is the most targeted for that exact phrase, but it still also contains the shorter terms.

So the usual pattern is:

- Exact-match longer phrase helps the exact phrase most.
- It also helps the shorter phrases inside it.
- Shorter, more generic anchors are less targeted for the longer queries.

But there are big modifiers:

- Link relevance matters a lot.
- Link authority matters a lot.
- A relevant, trusted site can outweigh many weak links.
- Anchor text is only one signal among many.

So if you had to think of it as a rough matrix:

- “widget” anchor: strongest for “widget,” weaker for the longer phrases
- “blue widget” anchor: strongest for “blue widget,” also helps “widget” and “best blue widget”
- “best blue widget” anchor: strongest for “best blue widget,” still helps the shorter phrases

- So if you put important content only inside an iframe, that content may not contribute much to the page’s rankings.

Important distinction:
- Old-style `frames` and `iframe`s are different technically, but for SEO they have similar problems.

  - good external signals
  - older/established site history

So the fact that a framed site ranks well does not mean frames are good for SEO. It just means SEO is influenced by many factors, and a weak SEO practice can sometimes still rank if the site is strong enough in other ways.

Best practice:
- Avoid using frames/iframes for primary page content
- Use normal HTML content directly in the page whenever possible
- If you must use an iframe, keep it for secondary content, not core SEO content

When Google says “0 search results found,” it means Google didn’t find any pages in its index that it considered relevant enough to show for that query.

Yes — to prevent one Apache virtual host from exposing another’s files, make sure each vhost has its own separate DocumentRoot and a unique ServerName.

Your problem happens because serverA’s DocumentRoot is the parent directory:

- serverA.com -> /var/www/html/
- serverB.com -> /var/www/html/serverB/

So Apache can still serve `/serverB/` as a subdirectory of serverA.

Fix:
1. Put each site in its own document root
2. Configure each vhost explicitly

Example:

<VirtualHost W.X.Y.Z:80>
    ServerName serverA.com
    DocumentRoot "/var/www/html/serverA"
</VirtualHost>

<VirtualHost W.X.Y.Z:80>
    ServerName serverB.com
    DocumentRoot "/var/www/html/serverB"
</VirtualHost>

Important points:
- Do not use a shared parent directory like `/var/www/html/` for one site if another site lives under it.
- `ServerName` must match the domain for that vhost.
- `DocumentRoot` must point only to that site’s directory.

If you also want to be extra safe, you can add a default catch-all vhost or directory access rules, but in most cases separating the DocumentRoots is the correct solution.

There isn’t a single “proper” cache time for `.htaccess`. The right value depends on how often each file changes.

General rule:

- **Static files that rarely change**: cache longer
  - images, fonts, versioned CSS/JS: days, weeks, even months
- **Files that may change often**: cache shorter
  - HTML, PHP output: hours or less, or don’t cache aggressively unless you control invalidation

Typical approach:

- **HTML/PHP**: short cache or no browser cache, because content often changes
- **CSS/JS**: longer cache, especially if filenames are versioned when updated
- **Images**: long cache, since they usually change infrequently

A practical guideline:

- Content changes daily: about **24 hours**
- Content changes weekly or less: **1–2 weeks**
- Stable assets with versioned filenames: **1 month or more**

The key is not “ideal” time, but whether users will get stale content. If you can rename files when they change, you can safely use much longer cache times.

- old-domain.com/page1 -> new-domain.com/page1

- domain forwarding with path preservation, or

- It has no built-in bulk redirect API for thousands of old URLs
- It won’t manage redirects for a domain it is no longer publishing to

Your `.htaccess` looks generally fine for browser caching of static files, but there are a couple of important points:

1. `mod_expires` only helps with browser caching
- It does not do full page caching.
- It tells browsers to keep copies of images, CSS, JS, etc. for a period of time.

2. Your rules are for static assets, not dynamic HTML
- `text/html "access 1 month"` may not be what you want for dynamically generated pages.
- If your site is PHP-driven, HTML pages are usually not cached this way unless you’re using a separate page-cache system.

3. Check whether caching is actually working
The resolved thread suggests that caching may already be active. To verify:
- Use Google PageSpeed Insights
- Use YSlow
- Check response headers in your browser dev tools

4. A better `.htaccess` structure
Keep rewrite rules and cache rules together, but make sure modules are enabled:
- `mod_rewrite`
- `mod_expires`

Example:

```apache
DirectoryIndex index.php

<IfModule mod_rewrite.c>
RewriteEngine On

RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} ^www\.decodinghinduism\.in [NC]
RewriteRule ^(.*)$ http://decodinghinduism.in/$1 [R=301,L]

RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-f
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-d
RewriteRule ^.*$ index.php?qa-rewrite=$0&%{QUERY_STRING} [L]
</IfModule>

<IfModule mod_expires.c>
ExpiresActive On
ExpiresByType image/jpg "access plus 1 year"
ExpiresByType image/jpeg "access plus 1 year"
ExpiresByType image/gif "access plus 1 year"
ExpiresByType image/png "access plus 1 year"
ExpiresByType text/css "access plus 1 month"
ExpiresByType application/javascript "access plus 1 month"
ExpiresByType text/javascript "access plus 1 month"
ExpiresByType image/x-icon "access plus 1 year"
ExpiresDefault "access plus 1 month"
</IfModule>
```

5. If you want true page caching
You need something beyond `.htaccess`, such as:
- CMS/plugin caching
- reverse proxy caching
- application-level caching
- server-side caching modules

So in short: your `.htaccess` can handle browser caching for static files, but it won’t fully cache pages. If you want, I can help you rewrite this `.htaccess` into a cleaner production-ready version.

- Do not use a site-wide canonical from one domain to another unless every page truly maps to its exact counterpart.
- If the domains are intended to be separate brands/features, make sure the unique parts are substantial enough to justify separate indexing.

In short: if the content is mostly the same, use canonical or noindex on the duplicate domain. If you want both domains to rank independently, they need significantly different content.

- Often the apex redirects to `www`, or `www` redirects to the apex, depending on your preference

Google’s Traffic Estimator is not giving you a fixed, “true” average CPC for that keyword. It is estimating the CPC you’d likely pay at a given bid level, and that estimate changes as your maximum CPC changes because the auction position, click volume, and competing bids all affect the model.

Why you see different numbers:

- At a very high max CPC, Google assumes you’re willing to bid enough to enter more auctions and possibly appear in higher positions.
- Higher positions usually get more clicks, but those clicks can also be more expensive.
- The estimated average CPC is then based on the mix of clicks Google expects you to receive at that bid.
- At a lower max CPC, you may only qualify for fewer, cheaper clicks, so the estimated average CPC can drop.

So in your example:

- Max CPC = AU$100 → estimated avg CPC = AU$6.08
- Max CPC = AU$10 → estimated avg CPC = AU$3.87

This does not mean Google is “charging” different averages for the same keyword in a simple linear way. It means the estimator is recalculating expected performance at different bid ceilings.

A few important notes:

- The Traffic Estimator is only a rough forecast, not a guaranteed prediction.
- It uses historical auction data, but actual results depend on Quality Score, ad relevance, landing page, competition, time of day, and other factors.
- For exact traffic to a website, Google Ads tools can only estimate ad traffic, not total organic website traffic.

If you mean “traffic to a website” in the general sense, you’d typically use:
- Google Analytics for your own site
- Search Console for organic search impressions/clicks
- Third-party tools like Similarweb, Semrush, Ahrefs, etc., for rough competitor estimates

If there is already a wildcard DNS record at that level, e.g. `*.domain.com`, then a specific subdomain like `sub.domain.com` cannot be set as a separate DNS alias unless your DNS server supports an explicit, more specific record that overrides the wildcard.

A few key points:

1. DNS only maps names to IPs/hosts
   - DNS cannot “redirect” one domain to another in the web sense.
   - It can only point `sub.domain.com` to an IP or hostname.

2. Specific records beat wildcard records
   - If your DNS zone allows it, create an explicit record for:
     - `sub.domain.com`
   - That record will usually override `*.domain.com`.

3. If you want the browser URL to stay as `sub.domain.com`
   - Use a reverse proxy on the server handling `sub.domain.com`.
   - That proxy forwards requests to `domain.org` while the browser still shows `sub.domain.com`.

Example Apache reverse proxy:

```apache
<VirtualHost *:80>
    ServerName sub.domain.com

    ProxyRequests Off
    ProxyPass / http://domain.org/
    ProxyPassReverse / http://domain.org/
</VirtualHost>
```

If you’re using HTTPS, you also need SSL configured on the proxy host.

4. If you only change DNS to point to the other server
   - The URL may still show `sub.domain.com` only if the web server on the target host is configured to answer for that hostname.
   - If it issues redirects, the browser may switch to `domain.org`.

5. If the wildcard already “captures” it
   - Check whether your DNS provider lets you add an explicit host record for `sub`.
   - If not, you may need to remove or adjust the wildcard.

Short answer:
- DNS alone cannot make `sub.domain.com` an alias of `domain.org` while keeping the `.com` in the browser.
- Use an explicit DNS record plus a reverse proxy if you want the URL preserved.

No — creating the Apache virtual host alone is not enough.

A subdomain like `sub.domain.com` must also exist in DNS. The browser first asks DNS for `sub.domain.com`; only after DNS returns an IP address does Apache get the request and decide which virtual host to use.

If you already have a wildcard DNS record like:

- `*.domain.com -> 1.2.3.4`

then `sub.domain.com` will already resolve to that server, so Apache virtual hosting is enough on the web server side.

But if you want `sub.domain.com` to behave as an alias of another domain, the DNS side must still point it at the same server, and then Apache should be configured with:

- a `ServerAlias sub.domain.com` on the target virtual host, or
- a separate vhost that redirects/proxies to the other domain

Important distinction:

- DNS: maps names to IPs
- Apache virtual hosts: maps hostnames to sites on that server
- `domain.com/sub` is a path, not a subdomain

So in short:

- If wildcard DNS already exists for that level, you may not need to change DNS.
- If there is no DNS record, Apache alone will not make the subdomain work.
- To make one hostname act like another, use `ServerAlias`, redirect, or proxy on Apache.

A wildcard DNS record does not automatically prevent you from creating a specific alias for a subdomain.

If you already have something like:

*.mydomain.com -> 1.2.3.4

you can still create a more specific record such as:

run.mydomain.com -> CNAME public.otherdomain.com

DNS matching is normally more specific records first, wildcard second. So `run.mydomain.com` will use the explicit record, and only subdomains without an explicit match will fall back to the wildcard.

- A CNAME cannot coexist with other records for the same exact name.

- Some DNS providers or zone managers may have interface restrictions, but the DNS standard allows this.
- If the wildcard is already `*.mydomain.com`, an explicit `run.mydomain.com` record should override it.

- During that time, some users will see old DNS and some new DNS.
- **Email is not normally lost** if the MX record is the same in both DNS zones and the old mail server stays online.
- If some senders still use the old DNS and others the new DNS, mail will still go to the same MX target, so it should be fine.

Yes, if you set up the new DNS zone first, you can test it by querying the new nameserver directly, for example with `dig` or `nslookup` against that server.

For the website, there may be a short period where different resolvers see different answers because of cached DNS.

For email, if MX stays the same and the mail server stays up, there should be **little to no downtime**.

If you do an MX lookup now, the result is the **mail server host name** used in the MX record, not the IP you should put directly into the MX record.

Google can show different titles for the search result and for the cached copy because they are generated in different ways.

- Search result title: Google usually uses the page title it indexed, but it may rewrite it based on the query, page content, links, or other signals.
- Cached page title: The cached version is a snapshot of how Google stored the page at crawl time, and the title shown there may reflect that older snapshot or Google’s cached display format.

So the two titles do not have to match exactly.

If your concern is only removing the “Cached” link, not the page from search results, use:

<meta name="robots" content="noarchive">

That prevents Google from offering the cached copy, but it does not remove the page from search listings.

- Put clear internal links to it from other important pages on your site
- Use descriptive title tags, headings, and copy focused on the target keyword

- Include it in your sitemap
- Earn external links pointing to that page
- Reduce competition from similar pages by consolidating overlapping content

- Return a 404 or 410 if the page is permanently gone
- Redirect to the most relevant matching page, if one exists
- Show a helpful “page removed” message with links to related content

Why this happens:
- Google may understand the page, but choose to rank the homepage instead.
- The page may have weak authority compared with the rest of the site.
- Other pages may not have enough internal links, backlinks, or trust signals.

What to do:
- Make sure each page has unique title tags and content.
- Add strong internal links to important pages.
- Build relevant backlinks to those pages from reputable sites/directories.
- Be patient: SEO changes can take a long time to reflect in results.

So the short answer is: the title is likely showing in Google’s index, but the page is not strong enough to rank in normal search results yet.

Search engines don’t let you say “rank this page above the other pages on my site” directly, and they also don’t really support “this section is random, don’t count it for ranking.”

If your goal is to get one specific page to outrank your other pages on the same site for a keyword, the practical ways are:

- Make that page the strongest match for the keyword:
  - Put the keyword in the title tag, H1, headings, and main body.
  - Make sure the page has the most relevant, unique content for that topic.
- Strengthen internal linking:
  - Link to that page from important pages on your site.
  - Use descriptive anchor text that matches the topic.
  - Reduce links pointing to competing pages with the same keyword focus.
- Avoid keyword cannibalization:
  - Don’t have multiple pages targeting the exact same query.
  - Consolidate similar content or use canonical tags if appropriate.
- Make the page more authoritative:
  - Get external links to that specific page.
  - Improve engagement and usefulness.

If you mean random content on a page is causing it to rank for terms that only appear sometimes, there’s no special “no-rank div” markup. Search engines mostly index the page as they see it. If that content should not influence rankings, the usual fix is:

- Remove it from the HTML source if possible
- Load it in a way search engines won’t index, if it’s truly not part of the page’s main content
- Mark the page more clearly with stable, relevant content
- Use `noindex` on pages that shouldn’t rank at all

So the short answer is: you can’t directly force one page to rank before another, and you can’t tag a div as “ignore for ranking.” You can only influence relevance and authority through content structure, internal linking, and site architecture.

3. The cached page may load some live resources
   - In some cases, the cached page can pull scripts/styles or other elements directly from the live site, which can make it look more current than the cached snippet/title.
