For an ever-changing part of the site, the main SEO concern is usually: don’t let Google see it as unstable, duplicated, or low-value.

Key things to handle:

1. Keep the changeable content in a stable URL
- Avoid creating a new URL every time the content changes.
- Use one canonical page and update the content behind it.

2. Use proper canonical tags
- If the content is republished, filtered, or available in multiple versions, point to the preferred URL.

3. Control indexing of variants
- If the changing content creates many near-duplicate pages, consider noindex, canonicalization, or parameter handling.

4. Make the page still meaningful on its own
- The page should have enough static context, text, and internal links so Google understands what it’s about even when the dynamic part changes.

5. Avoid thin or empty states
- If the page sometimes loads with little content, make sure the core content is present in HTML or server-side rendered, not only after JavaScript runs.

6. Update XML sitemaps and lastmod correctly
- If content changes often and materially, keep the sitemap signals accurate.
- Don’t overdo change signals if the URL itself doesn’t meaningfully change.

7. Protect against crawl inefficiency
- If the ever-changing area creates lots of crawlable URLs, faceted links, or calendar-style pages, limit wasteful crawl paths.

8. Preserve internal linking
- Link to the main evergreen page from relevant sections so authority keeps flowing to the right URL.

9. If it’s time-sensitive, mark it clearly
- For content like events, listings, stock, jobs, or schedules, use appropriate structured data and visible dates/status.

10. Decide whether it should be indexable at all
- If the content changes too frequently to be useful in search, it may be better as a utility page rather than a target for organic traffic.

If Google is not reading your website’s title, meta tags, description, or page content correctly, the issue is usually not that Google “ignores” them — it’s that Googlebot is not seeing the same HTML that users see.

Most common reasons:

- Googlebot is getting an error page instead of the real page
  - 4xx/5xx errors
  - timeouts
  - blocked by WAF, firewall, CDN, security plugin, or bot protection
- The page is inconsistent
  - sometimes correct HTML
  - sometimes redirect, soft 404, or error page
- The content is loaded only by JavaScript
  - Google may not render it the way your browser does
- The page is being cached or served differently to bots
- Meta tags are missing in the raw HTML and added only after JavaScript runs

What to check:

1. View the page source
   - Make sure the title tag, meta description, and important content are present in the raw HTML, not just visible in the browser.

2. Test the HTTP response
   - Confirm the page returns 200 OK
   - Make sure Googlebot is not getting a different response than normal visitors

3. Use Google Search Console
   - URL Inspection
   - Test Live URL
   - Inspect the rendered HTML and screenshot
   - Request indexing after fixing issues

4. Check server logs
   - Look for Googlebot requests
   - See whether they receive 200, 403, 404, 500, or timeout responses

5. Review CDN / firewall / security settings
   - Cloudflare, WAF, bot protection, caching rules, or plugin filters may block or alter what Google sees

6. Make sure important SEO tags are server-rendered
   - Title tag
   - Meta description
   - Canonical tag
   - Main content

Important note:
If Google can crawl the page but still does not use your title or description, Google may rewrite them based on what it thinks is more relevant. That can happen even when everything is technically working.

In short:
Google is probably not “missing” your title/meta tags — it is likely receiving the wrong page version, an error, or rendered content that is not present in the initial HTML. Make sure the page reliably returns the correct server-rendered HTML with HTTP 200, then request reindexing in Search Console.

Google may still be crawling your page correctly, but showing a different title/description in search results.

This is common. Google often rewrites:
- the page title
- the meta description
- sometimes even the snippet text

based on what it thinks is more relevant to the user’s search.

Why this happens:
- Your title may be too long, repetitive, or keyword-stuffed
- Your meta description may not match the page content well
- Google may find on-page text more useful than your meta tags
- The page content may not clearly match the title/description theme

- Write a unique meta description for each page

- Avoid stuffing keywords in title/description
- Use proper headings (`H1`, `H2`) that reflect the page topic

Important:
- Google does not always display your exact title or meta description
- This does not necessarily mean Google is not reading them
- There is no guaranteed way to force Google to use your exact text in search results

Google can’t reliably be told to ignore only part of a page. Search engines generally index a page as a whole, not individual sections.

What you can do instead:

- Put the sensitive content on a separate URL
- Keep that URL out of search results by:
  - blocking it in `robots.txt`
  - or adding `noindex` to that page

A few caveats:

- `robots.txt` prevents crawling, but doesn’t guarantee removal if Google already knows the URL
- `noindex` works on the whole page, not just one section
- Hiding content with CSS or JavaScript is not a reliable way to keep it out of indexing

So the practical solution is to split the content into its own page/resource and exclude that page from indexing.

After 6 months of downtime, the situation is more like a site relaunch/recovery than a normal SEO fluctuation. If the domain or site was changed, the key question is whether search engines can clearly understand that the new site is the same entity and that old URLs map to new ones.

What to do:

1. Rebuild and keep the old URLs accessible via 301 redirects
- Redirect every old important URL to the most relevant new URL.
- Avoid redirecting everything to the homepage.
- Remove redirect chains and loops.

2. Make sure the site is fully crawlable and indexable
- Check robots.txt, meta robots tags, canonical tags, and noindex rules.
- Ensure important pages return 200 status codes.
- Submit a clean XML sitemap.

3. Verify the site in Google Search Console
- Add both old and new domains if applicable.
- Submit the sitemap for the current site.
- Use the Change of Address tool if you changed domains and the old domain still exists.
- Review indexing, coverage, and crawl stats.

4. Restore the original content and page structure where possible
- Keep the same page topics, URLs, titles, and internal linking patterns if you can.
- If content changed significantly, rankings may not return the same way.

5. Check for lost backlinks and signals
- Update important backlinks you control to point to the new URLs.
- Make sure redirects pass users and crawlers cleanly.

6. Fix technical issues from the downtime
- Verify server reliability, page speed, mobile usability, and HTTPS.
- Make sure no pages are accidentally blocked or missing.

7. Expect recovery to take time
- After 6 months offline, rankings and traffic may not come back quickly.
- Search engines may need to reprocess the site and reassign trust signals.
- Some pages may recover, while others may not fully return.

8. Monitor what Google is actually indexing
- Look at indexed pages, impressions, queries, and pages that dropped hardest.
- Focus first on pages that used to drive the most traffic and links.

HTTPS migration should not create a duplicate-content problem if it’s handled correctly.

The key is to make HTTPS the single canonical version of every page:

- 301 redirect all HTTP URLs to the matching HTTPS URLs
- Update all internal links to HTTPS
- Make sure canonical tags, hreflang, XML sitemaps, and structured data reference HTTPS
- Add and verify the HTTPS property in Google Search Console
- Clear any CDN/cache after the switch

Why this works:
- HTTP and HTTPS are different URLs
- If both are accessible, search engines may see them as duplicates
- A permanent 301 redirect tells search engines the HTTP version has moved to HTTPS
- Over time, ranking signals consolidate to the HTTPS pages

What to avoid:
- Leaving both HTTP and HTTPS pages live without redirects
- Mixing signals, such as HTTP internal links with HTTPS canonicals
- Forgetting to update sitemaps or structured data

Best practice:
1. Install the SSL certificate
2. Set up 301 redirects from HTTP to HTTPS
3. Change internal links to HTTPS
4. Update canonicals to HTTPS
5. Update XML sitemap URLs to HTTPS
6. Resubmit the sitemap in Search Console
7. Monitor indexing and crawl errors after launch

So, the SEO-safe approach is simply to enforce HTTPS site-wide with proper 301 redirects and consistent canonical signals.

```html
<meta name="robots" content="noindex, nofollow">
```

```http
X-Robots-Tag: noindex, nofollow
```

This is the most reliable method:
- HTTP basic auth
- password protection
- staging environment access restrictions

3. Use robots.txt only as a secondary measure
You can add:

```txt
User-agent: *
Disallow: /
```

- Use Google Search Console’s Removals tool for temporary removal
- Keep `noindex` in place for permanent removal

Important distinction
- `robots.txt` = controls crawling
- `noindex` = controls indexing

To hide your website or specific pages from search engines using `robots.txt`, add rules that disallow crawling of the URLs you want excluded.

Example:

```txt
User-agent: *
Disallow: /
```

This tells all search engine bots not to crawl any part of the site.

If you only want to hide certain sections or pages:

```txt
User-agent: *
Disallow: /private/
Disallow: /secret-page.html
```

A few important notes:

- `robots.txt` only blocks crawling, not guaranteed indexing
- If a URL is already known, it may still appear in search results without a snippet
- For full removal from search results, use `noindex` on the page itself, or remove the page entirely
- `robots.txt` cannot hide only part of a page; it works at the URL/path level

If you want, I can help you write the exact `robots.txt` rules for your site structure.

If you mean short-lived URLs like expiring links, temporary campaign URLs, or signed URLs, the best SEO approach is usually to avoid making them indexable at all.

What to do:

1. Use a permanent canonical URL
- Point SEO authority to the stable, long-term URL.
- Example: /product/widget instead of /promo/widget?token=abc123

2. Keep temporary URLs out of the index
- If the URL is only meant for a short time, set noindex if it can be crawled.
- For truly private or signed URLs, use robots controls plus proper access restrictions.

3. Redirect expired URLs to the best permanent page
- If the short-lived URL had public value, redirect it to the main equivalent page.
- Usually use 301 if the replacement is permanent.

4. Don’t rely on short-lived URLs for ranking
- Search engines prefer stable URLs.
- A URL that disappears quickly won’t build lasting SEO value.

5. Make the target page descriptive
- Since the URL itself has limited SEO impact, the permanent destination should have:
  - a clear title,
  - good headings,
  - useful content,
  - internal links,
  - and external links if possible.

If you’re asking about “short lifetime” in the sense of URLs that expire after a few minutes/hours, the best practice is:
- keep them non-indexable,
- redirect or replace them with a permanent URL,
- and make the permanent URL the one you optimize for SEO.

To keep search engines from indexing specific content on your site, use one of these methods:

   ```http
   X-Robots-Tag: noindex, nofollow
   ```

2. Protect the content with authentication
   - Best option if the content should not be public at all
   - Use password protection, HTTP basic auth, or staging access restrictions

3. Use `robots.txt` as a secondary measure only
   - Example:
   ```txt
   User-agent: *
   Disallow: /private/
   ```
   - Note: `robots.txt` stops crawling, not indexing, so it is not enough by itself for content already known to search engines

Important distinction:
- `noindex` = tells search engines not to index the page
- `robots.txt` = tells search engines not to crawl the page

If the content is already indexed, use:
- `noindex` on the page for permanent removal
- Google Search Console’s Removals tool for temporary hiding

You can’t force Google to use a specific `<description>` tag in search results, but you can strongly influence the snippet it shows.

What to do in PHP/HTML:
- Add a unique `<title>` for each page/sub-page
- Add a unique meta description in the `<head>`

Example:
```html
<head>
  <title>My Subpage Title</title>
  <meta name="description" content="Short, clear description of this subpage for search engines.">
</head>
```

If you’re generating pages in PHP:
```php
<head>
  <title><?= htmlspecialchars($title) ?></title>
  <meta name="description" content="<?= htmlspecialchars($description) ?>">
</head>
```

Important:
- Google may ignore your meta description and generate its own snippet
- It does not read a `<description>` tag unless you mean `<meta name="description">`
- Make sure each sub-page has its own relevant description
- Keep the visible page content aligned with the description

If you want, I can show you how to set dynamic meta descriptions in a PHP template.

Google may be showing a different snippet or description than the one you set, and that’s normal.

A few things can cause this:

- Google can rewrite the page title in search results.
- Google can replace your meta description with text from the page if it thinks that text is more relevant to the search.
- A “strange” description doesn’t necessarily mean something is broken.

Common reasons:
- The title is too long, repetitive, or keyword-stuffed
- The title doesn’t match the page content closely
- The meta description is missing, duplicated, or not specific enough
- Google finds another part of the page more relevant to the query
- The page isn’t fully indexed yet

What to check:
1. Open the page source and confirm:
   - `<title>`
   - `<meta name="description">`
   - main visible content

2. Check Google Search Console:
   - URL Inspection
   - whether the page is indexed
   - request indexing if needed

3. Improve the title and meta description:
   - make them unique
   - keep them clear and relevant
   - avoid making them too long
   - make sure they match the page content

4. Make sure the main text is crawlable:
   - not hidden in scripts
   - not only loaded after interaction
   - not blocked by robots.txt or a noindex tag

If you want, send me:
- the page URL
- the exact title tag
- the meta description

Then I can help you figure out whether Google is rewriting the snippet and what to change.

Google can’t reliably be told to ignore only part of a page. Search engines generally index a page as a whole, not individual sections.

What you can do instead:

- Put the content you want hidden on a separate URL
- Keep that URL out of search results by:
  - blocking it in `robots.txt`
  - or adding `noindex` to that page

A few caveats:

- `robots.txt` prevents crawling, but doesn’t guarantee removal if Google already knows the URL
- `noindex` works on the whole page, not just one section
- Hiding content with CSS or JavaScript is not a reliable way to keep it out of indexing

So the practical solution is to split the content into its own page/resource and exclude that page from indexing.

What matters most:
1. Attribution and links

- Text that is visible in the widget on the other site may not be counted as much as content on your own pages.
- Search engines may ignore or devalue repeated widget content if it appears across many sites.

- Bad: `/blog/content strategy!/`

- `/blog/category/post-title/`

If the file is already showing up in Google, the reliable way to hide it is to keep that file on its own URL and prevent that URL from being indexed.

Options:

1. Add `noindex` to the file’s page/resource
   - This tells Google not to index that URL.
   - Works best if Google can still crawl the page.

2. Block it in `robots.txt`
   - This can stop crawling.
   - But if Google already knows the URL, it may still appear in results for a while.

Important:
- Google can’t reliably hide only part of a page or file.
- `noindex` applies to the whole page/file URL, not just a section.
- Hiding with CSS/JavaScript is not a reliable way to keep it out of search results.

For short-lifetime URLs, the best SEO approach is usually:

1. Keep the URL permanent if possible
- If the page may be reused, don’t change the URL unless you have to.
- A stable URL accumulates links and trust over time.

2. If the content is temporary, don’t rely on the URL for SEO
- For things like promos, events, or time-sensitive pages, the content matters more than the URL.
- Use a clear, descriptive URL, but don’t over-optimize it.

3. Use a redirect if the page moves or expires
- If the URL is replaced by a newer page, use a 301 redirect to the closest relevant permanent page.
- Avoid letting valuable short-lived URLs just disappear with 404s if they earned links or traffic.

4. If the page should not stay indexed, use noindex
- For truly temporary pages that shouldn’t remain in search results, add noindex.
- You can keep the page accessible for users while preventing long-term indexing.

5. Avoid putting dates or expirations in URLs unless necessary
- Dates can make URLs feel stale and reduce reuse.
- A cleaner URL is better if the same topic may return later.

Best practice:
- Permanent topic page: short, descriptive, stable URL
- Temporary campaign/event page: short, descriptive URL + redirect/noindex plan
- Expired content: redirect to the most relevant live page

Example:
- Good: example.com/summer-sale
- Better than: example.com/summer-sale-2024-07
- If it expires, redirect example.com/summer-sale to the current sale or a relevant category page

Best practices:

    - /fr/
    - /de/
  - Avoid requiring form input, session state, or JavaScript-only filters to reveal locale-specific data.

- Make localized pages easy to link to
  - Use standard `<a>` links between language/region versions.
  - Put alternate language/region links in the page markup.

- Use `hreflang` for language/region targeting
  - This helps search engines understand which version is for which audience.
  - Example:
    ```html
    <link rel="alternate" hreflang="en" href="https://example.com/en/" />
    <link rel="alternate" hreflang="fr" href="https://example.com/fr/" />
    <link rel="alternate" hreflang="de" href="https://example.com/de/" />
    ```

- Make sure each localized page has unique, descriptive titles and content
  - Don’t rely on the same generic page for every region.

- Add localized pages to your XML sitemap
  - Submit the sitemap in Google Search Console.
  - Include all important locale URLs.

- Avoid blocking localized content
  - Check `robots.txt`, `noindex`, canonical tags, and redirects.
  - Make sure the versions you want indexed are reachable without restrictions.

- Serve content server-side where possible
  - Search engines should be able to see the localized content in the initial HTML, not only after client-side rendering.

- Provide location signals where relevant
  - Local business info, country-specific contact details, currency, addresses, and local phone numbers can help.

- Test what search engines see
  - Use Google Search Console’s URL Inspection tool to verify the rendered HTML and indexed page.
  - Make sure the crawler sees the localized content you expect.
